extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of social institutions, political science, and rhetoric; educated general readers
extracted.subtask_description: Criteria and standards for evaluating public speaking (oratory): the aptitudes, stylistic qualities, delivery traits, common defects, and relative strengths that constitute oratorical excellence, as discussed in a late-19th/early-20th-century social-institutions text. Also includes related discussion of the social/political role of a capital city.

rubrics_metrics.name: Invention (finding good ideas and weaving effective arguments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Invention, that is, the power of finding good ideas and weaving effective arguments.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Listed as one of five core aptitudes of oratorical excellence. Tied to the speaker's intellectual resources and capacity for substantive material.

rubrics_metrics.name: Choice of appropriate words (skill and taste)
rubrics_metrics.description: Skill and taste in the choice of appropriate words.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of the five aptitudes; pertains to literary form and diction rather than merely delivery. The text notes American speakers are not necessarily superior in literary form.

rubrics_metrics.name: Readiness in producing ideas and words at short notice
rubrics_metrics.description: Readiness in producing appropriate ideas and words at short notice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of the five aptitudes; identified as a strength of American speakers (part of the three latter aptitudes in which Americans excel).

rubrics_metrics.name: Quickness in catching the temper of the audience
rubrics_metrics.description: Quickness in catching the temper and tendencies of the particular audience addressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of the five aptitudes; emphasizes audience awareness and adaptation; regarded as a distinguishing American advantage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Delivery: weight, animation, and grace
rubrics_metrics.description: Weight, animation, and grace in delivery.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: One of the five aptitudes; delivery qualities (including animation and grace) are central to oratorical excellence and a noted American strength.

rubrics_metrics.name: Relative emphasis on improvisation, audience-adaptation, and delivery
rubrics_metrics.description: Such excellence as the Americans possess ... consists rather in the three latter of these than in the two former.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance on relative importance: Americans tend to excel more in readiness, audience-sensitivity, and delivery than in invention and literary choice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Substance depends on intellectual resources and audience capacity
rubrics_metrics.description: The substance of their speeches is not better than one finds in other countries, because substance depends on the intellectual resources of the speaker and on the capacity of the audience for appreciating worthy matter.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluative principle: assess speech substance by speaker's underlying intellectual resources and the audience's ability to appreciate it, not by rhetorical flourishes.

rubrics_metrics.name: Fluency, readiness, and self-possession
rubrics_metrics.description: There is more fluency, more readiness, more self-possession.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aspects of effective oratory: fluid delivery and composure are positive markers; linked to greater practice and familiarity with speaking occasions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of humour to maintain audience contact
rubrics_metrics.description: Humour, which is a commoner gift in America than elsewhere, often redeems an otherwise uninteresting address, and is the best means of keeping speaker and audience in touch with one another.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical guidance: employ humour as a device to engage listeners and redeem weak material; especially valuable for maintaining rapport.

rubrics_metrics.name: Deliberate and even slow delivery as an advantage
rubrics_metrics.description: A deliberate and even slow delivery is the rule in American public speaking ... This has the advantage of making a story or a jest tell with more effect.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Style guidance: prefer measured pacing to allow stories and jokes to land; slow delivery aids clarity and effect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Less stiffness, greater voice management and enunciation
rubrics_metrics.description: There is also, I think, less stiffness and hesitation among American than among English speakers, greater skill in managing the voice, because more practice in open-air meetings, greater clearness of enunciation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate speakers for naturalness, vocal control, and clear enunciation; these traits increase effectiveness and stem from practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid turgid, inflated, or florid rhetoric
rubrics_metrics.description: The commonest American defect used to be a turgid and inflated style. The rhetoric was Rhodian rather than Attic, overloaded with tropes and figures, apt to aim at concealing poverty or triteness in thought by exaggeration of statement, by a profusion of ornament, by appeals to sentiments loftier than the subject or the occasion required.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anti-pattern: avoid excessive ornament, exaggerated appeals, or florid diction when clarity or cogency is required. Match rhetorical tone to subject and occasion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Appropriate matching of rhetorical form to purpose (clarity over ornament)
rubrics_metrics.description: Too frequently the florid diction of the debating club or the solemn pomp of the funeral oration was invoked when nothing but clearness of exposition or cogency of argument was needed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Guidance to assess whether rhetorical form suits purpose: favor clear exposition and cogent argument over pomp where appropriate.

rubrics_metrics.name: Definition and characteristics of a Capital city
rubrics_metrics.description: By a Capital I mean a city which is not only the seat of political government, but is also by the size, wealth, and character of its population the head and centre of the country, a leading seat of commerce and industry, a reservoir of financial resources, the favoured residence of the great and powerful, the spot in which the chiefs of the learned professions are to be found, where the most potent and widely read journals are published, whither men of literary and scientific capacity are drawn.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these characteristics to evaluate whether a city functions as a national capital in the cultural, political, economic, and intellectual senses.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital's role in shaping political opinion and initiative
rubrics_metrics.description: The opinion of such a city becomes powerful politically because it is that of the persons who live at headquarters ... these members of the legislature reside in the capital, and cannot but feel the steady pressure of its prevailing sentiment which touches them socially at every point.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Evaluate the capital's influence by its ability to concentrate elites, shape legislative behaviour, and act as a source of political initiative and diffusion.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capital as a foundry for art and literature (creative concentration)
rubrics_metrics.description: In the field of art and literature the influence of a great capital is no less marked. It gathers to a centre the creative power of the country, and subjects it to the criticism of the best instructed and most polished society. The constant action and reaction ... may give birth to works which isolated genius could hardly have produced.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess cultural dynamism by degree of artistic concentration, critical interchange, and the fostering of collaborative/competitive creative environments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Potential downside of centralization: diminished variety vs. higher efficiency
rubrics_metrics.description: The growth of such a centre may impoverish the rest of a country because the concentration of intellectual life tends to diminish the chances of variability, and establish too uniform a type; some compensation for any such loss may be found in the higher efficiency which such a society gives to the men of capacity whom it draws into its own orbit.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating centralization, weigh loss of regional variety and diversity against gains in critical mass, efficiency, and concentrated development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Effects of absence of a capital on public opinion (slower, more amorphous)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a natural result ... that in the United States public opinion crystallizes both less rapidly and in less sharp and well-defined forms than happens in those European countries which are led by the capital.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use this as an analytic criterion: dispersed centers produce slower, less sharply defined national opinions; evaluate political cultures accordingly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Democratic gains from a dispersed civic structure
rubrics_metrics.description: It is a gain that the multitude of no one city should be able to overawe the executive and the legislature ... It is a gain ... that the feeling of what is called Society ... should not become too marked and palpable in its influence on the members of the legislature and the administration, that it should rather be diffused over the nation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Assess benefits of dispersion: reduced risk of elite overreach, more diffuse social influence, and opinions more representative of varied classes and interests.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical criteria for choosing seats of government (centrality and insulation)
rubrics_metrics.description: The seat of Federal government was in 1790 fixed at a place which was not even a village ... not merely for the sake of preventing the national legislature from being threatened by the mob of a great city, but because the jealousies of the States made it necessary to place the legislature in a spot exempt from all State influence or jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When evaluating or designing government seats, consider central location, insulation from dominant local interests, and political compromises to prevent regional dominance.
